title: From Dubai to Arkansas: How an Indian Chef Conquered the World Food Championships
excerpt: Self-taught vegetarian chef Surabhi Suri became World Vegetarian Champion at the 2026 World Food Championships, carrying Indian culinary traditions onto the global stage.
body:
The world's largest food competition crowned an unexpected champion this month — and her secret weapon was a lifetime of vegetarian cooking rooted in her Indian grandmother's kitchen.

## A Self-Taught Chef on the Biggest Stage

Surabhi Suri, a Dubai-based Indian chef and founder of the supper club Sebzee, was proclaimed World Vegetarian Champion and First Runner-Up overall at the 2026 World Food Championships in Bentonville, Arkansas. The competition drew over 1,500 chefs from across the globe, making her achievement all the more remarkable.

What makes Suri's story extraordinary isn't just the win — it's how she got there. A self-taught cook who honed her craft through Dubai's multicultural dining scene, Suri competed in non-vegetarian rounds despite being a lifelong vegetarian herself. She prepared meat dishes through rigorous technical study: watching hundreds of technique videos, visiting professional kitchens, and using thermometers and feedback from sous chefs to perfect seasoning and doneness.

"I knew that most chefs in the competition would cook the meat perfectly," Suri told journalists after the competition. "But my upper hand was bringing that level of precision, creativity, and complexity to the plant-forward components of the dish. That balance became my edge."

## Indian Flavours Meet Global Ambition

Suri's winning dishes reflected a fusion of Indian and Mediterranean influences — a signature she developed during her years in Dubai. Her standout Beetroot Kofta dish, which clinched the vegetarian title, drew on traditional Indian kofta preparations while incorporating global plating techniques and flavour combinations.

The competition's judges were particularly impressed by her sides: an electric pea purée and grilled carrots topped with salsa verde that complemented her main dishes so seamlessly that they remarked her accompaniments tasted "nearly identical" in quality to the featured proteins.

Her journey mirrors a broader trend of Indian chefs gaining international recognition. At the same event, Texas chef Preston Nguyen ultimately claimed the overall $100,000 World Food Champion title, defeating Suri and fellow finalist David Casey in a grueling two-day finale. But Suri's vegetarian category dominance sent a powerful message about the sophistication of plant-forward Indian cooking.

## The Diaspora Connection

For the estimated 4.4 million Indian Americans and millions more NRIs worldwide, Suri's story resonates on multiple levels. She represents the dual identity many in the diaspora navigate — rooted in Indian traditions but shaped by global experiences.

"India is the origin of my cooking roots," Suri said. "I grew up, matured, and found my voice as a chef in the UAE." She credits her grandmother for teaching her patience, instinct, and respect for ingredients — the emotional foundations that, combined with Dubai's cosmopolitan food scene, forged her distinctive style.

Her win also challenges long-standing stereotypes about vegetarian cooking being somehow less impressive or technically demanding than meat-based cuisine. With India home to the world's largest vegetarian population, Suri's championship is a validation of a culinary philosophy that millions of diaspora families carry with them.

## What's Next

Suri has spoken about her ambition to open a zero-waste restaurant focused on mindful sourcing and sustainable vegetarian cuisine. Her success at the World Food Championships has already attracted international attention, and she hopes to inspire young expats and women in particular to pursue their culinary ambitions.

"There is no need to fit into traditional boxes as a path for success," she said. "Your strength is your unique self, your culture, and your voice. Dream big, hustle harder, and never be afraid to take space in the world."

For the diaspora, it's a reminder that Indian food — and Indian cooks — belong on the world's biggest stages.
